description: My name is Shurooq. I am interested in programming, graphic design, and technology. I have participated in several hackathons and gained experience in developing innovative projects. I also programmed a robot for a competitive game between two teams. I enjoy learning new skills and turning creative ideas into real projects.
summary:
What we built. PLANET OPS is an interactive 3D browser game that puts the player in the role of a junior astronaut trainer. Across five stages (the Moon, Mars and Venus, the asteroid belt, an icy moon of Jupiter, and deep space) the player inspects the spacecraft after every landing, faces realistic problems such as lost communications, low oxygen, sandstorms and radiation, and moves under each planet's own gravity. Along the way the player discovers 13 real pieces of equipment that NASA left behind.
How it addresses the challenge. The challenge asks for storytelling about NASA's discarded equipment. Each artifact becomes a 3D object in the game world. When the player approaches it, the game pauses and shows a short fact card based on NASA's NSSDCA catalog: what the equipment did and how it came to rest there, from Apollo's Eagle to the Sojourner rover and the Ingenuity helicopter. Each artifact appears where it really is, and the final screen shows how many of the 13 were found.
Why it matters. These artifacts are part of the history of space exploration, and their stories are rarely told. Learning through play helps students remember them, because they live the story instead of reading it. It also introduces young people to the idea of mission training and brings NASA's achievements together in one place.
details:
What it does and how it works. PLANET OPS is a 3D browser game where the player is a junior astronaut trainer. The player moves with an on-screen joystick or keyboard, solves problems such as lost communications, low oxygen, sandstorms and radiation, and inspects the spacecraft after every landing. When the player approaches a real piece of NASA equipment, the game pauses and shows a fact card from NSSDCA data.

Benefits. Students learn the history of NASA's discarded equipment by discovering it, practice decision-making under pressure (oxygen, fuel, comms), and see how planets differ in gravity, temperature and pressure. It needs no install: one link works on a phone or computer.

Intended impact. Keep the stories of these artifacts alive, make space and astronaut training appealing to students, and introduce NASA's achievements through play.

Tools and technologies. HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Three.js r128 (WebGL); Canvas 2D for procedural planet, fabric and terrain textures; Web Audio for sound effects; ffmpeg and Python for asset processing; NASA's NSSDCA catalog and the challenge's equipment list as data. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant, which should be disclosed under the competition's AI-use rules. Tested on iPad and phone browsers.

Why it is creative. It turns a data catalog into an explorable world instead of a reading list, combines mission training with storytelling, generates planets and textures in code so the whole game runs from one link, and carries decisions across stages.

Factors we considered. Accuracy (each artifact appears where it really is, with its source), mentor and judge feedback (faster pacing with a ×4/×2/×1 speed toggle, more realism, cleaner controls), mobile performance, touch-friendly controls, content suitability, and rights (a fan-made concept, not affiliated with NASA, with no NASA logo).
